t: Aim and plan of the session
n: The topic of this session: isolation of diuretic drug substances from biological objects and their analysis by the thin-layer chromatography screening method. The aim is to familiarise students with the toxicological significance and the methods of analysis of the drugs furosemide and acetazolamide. According to the plan, we will consider the toxicological significance of furosemide and acetazolamide and the methods of their analysis.

By the end of the session, students master the conditions for detecting furosemide and acetazolamide in pure solutions and in an unknown solution by qualitative reactions. They learn to isolate furosemide from blood and urine. Acetazolamide they learn to isolate from blood, urine and a biological object, that is the liver. In the screening analysis they identify the spot with Rf=0.55 and compare it with the standard.

Items needed for the work: test tubes, separating funnels, reagents and visual aids. The session is held in a room equipped with special laboratory facilities. Also needed are 50 ml and 25 ml volumetric flasks, a separating funnel, a porcelain dish, universal indicator paper, and Silufol and KSK plates. For isolation from the liver, an electric shaker, a gauze filter and a centrifuge running at 3000 rpm are used.

Reagents. Acetonitrile is taken for the standard solution. For extraction, diethyl ether, ethyl acetate-isopropyl alcohol 4:1, 10% and saturated NaCl, and dry Na2SO4 are needed. To adjust the pH, concentrated HCl and 0.2 N and 0.1 N HCl solutions are used. For thin-layer chromatography, the systems chloroform-toluene-ethanol-25% ammonia 15:5:30:2 and benzene-2-propanol 8:2 are taken. Developing reagents: 5% iron (III) chloride and Dragendorff reagent according to Munier.

Rules of safety and preparation. For the laboratory work the student brings rubber gloves, a wipe and a face mask. The examination is carried out in rooms with ventilation and a fume cupboard, which are locked and sealed when the work is finished. Objects from infected persons, that is those with tuberculosis, hepatitis and AIDS, arrive in a special container and are noted in the documents.

Classification of diuretic agents. Diuretics are divided into xanthine derivatives, carbonic anhydrase inhibitors, thiazides and potassium-sparing agents. According to the table, the carbonic anhydrase inhibitor group contains acetazolamide and the osmotic diuretics. The thiazide group includes hydrochlorothiazide. Potassium-sparing agents include spironolactone and triamterene. Furosemide and ethacrynic acid are given together with the thiazides in brackets, in the place of the loop diuretics.

Toxicological significance of diuretics. In the heart and blood vessels, a fall in blood pressure, tachycardia, collapse, arrhythmia and aplastic anaemia are observed. In metabolism, hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, hyperglycaemia, raised cholesterol and gout appear. In the gastrointestinal tract, loss of appetite, dry mouth, severe thirst, nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea and pancreatitis occur. In the nervous system and sense organs there are dizziness, drowsiness, muscle relaxation, impairment of hearing and vision, and also allergic reactions.

t: Isolation conditions: pH and salt amounts
n: Isolation conditions. For furosemide, blood is brought to pH=2.0 and urine to pH=2.0-3.0. For acetazolamide, blood and urine are brought to pH=3.0-4.0. To blood, 2 g of 10% NaCl is added, and to urine 2 g of NaCl. The extract is passed through a filter with 5.0 g of dry Na2SO4. Remember: the pH values for furosemide and acetazolamide are different.

t: Isolation by the aqueous acetone method
n: Isolation by the aqueous acetone method. The object is soaked in an acetone-water 5:3 mixture and saturated with NaCl. The acetone is evaporated, and the aqueous layer is extracted with ethyl acetate under acidic and alkaline conditions. The alkaline aqueous layer is re-extracted with chloroform. The organic layers are purified by thin-layer chromatography.

t: Aqueous acetone method from liver: steps
n: The steps of the aqueous acetone method from liver. 50 g of minced liver and 50 ml of acetone are placed in a 100 ml flask and mixed for 1 hour on an electric shaker. A further 50 ml of acetone is added to the solid part and shaken for 30 minutes; this process is repeated twice. The acetone layers are combined and centrifuged for 5 minutes at 3000 rpm. Saturated NaCl solution is added to the centrifugate, the acetone is evaporated on a water bath, and the aqueous part at pH 3.0-4.0 is extracted with ethyl acetate-isopropanol 4:1.

Standard solution of furosemide. 0.05 g of furosemide sample is placed in a 50 ml volumetric flask and dissolved in 5 ml of acetonitrile. The solution is made up to the mark. Then 1 ml of the solution is made up to the mark with acetonitrile in a 25 ml flask. That is, the standard is prepared in two stages, by dilution.

Isolating furosemide from blood. 5 ml of blood is brought to pH=2.0 with concentrated HCl, 2 g of 10% NaCl is added, and it is left to settle. The clear part is extracted twice in a funnel with 10 ml of diethyl ether. The extracts are passed through a filter with 5.0 g of dry Na2SO4 and dried at room temperature.

t: Furosemide: comparing isolation from blood and urine
n: Let us compare the isolation of furosemide from blood and urine. For blood: 5 ml of blood is brought to pH=2.0 with concentrated HCl, and 2 g of 10% NaCl is added. For urine: 2 g of NaCl is added to 25 ml of urine, and it is brought to pH=2.0-3.0 with 0.2 N HCl. In both cases extraction is carried out with 10 ml of diethyl ether. For blood, extraction is done twice.

Isolating furosemide from urine. 2 g of NaCl is added to a 25 ml urine sample and mixed until completely dissolved. The pH is brought to 2.0-3.0 with 0.2 N HCl, using universal indicator. Then extraction is carried out with 10 ml of diethyl ether. The extract is passed through a filter with 5.0 g of Na2SO4 and dried.

Chromatographic purification of furosemide. The residue is dissolved in 5 ml of acetone and applied to the start line of a Silufol plate as a band 1-2 cm wide. The plate is kept in a chamber with chloroform-toluene-ethanol-25% ammonia 15:5:30:2 until the front rises to 10 cm. With 5% FeCl3 a brown spot forms, Rf=0.55. The eluate is dissolved in 25 ml of ethyl alcohol.

The figures for thin-layer chromatography of furosemide. Chromatography is run in a chamber with chloroform-toluene-ethanol-25% ammonia 15:5:30:2 to 10 cm. The width of the start line is 1-2 cm. The developing reagent is 5% iron (III) chloride; the brown spot has Rf=0.55. The eluate is taken from the spot area and dissolved in 25 ml of ethyl alcohol.

The screening method for furosemide. The test solution is applied to a KSK plate as a dot, and the standard is applied beside it. The plate is chromatographed in a chamber with chloroform-toluene-ethanol-25% ammonia 15:5:30:2; fluorescence is observed in ultraviolet light. If a brown spot forms with 5% iron (III) chloride, Rf=0.55, this indicates the presence of furosemide in the solution.

The scheme for developing furosemide in a thin layer. The plate is viewed in ultraviolet light and fluorescence is observed. When sprayed with 5% iron (III) chloride, a brown-coloured spot forms, Rf=0.55. If the spot coincides with the standard, the presence of furosemide in the solution is established.

Authenticity reactions of furosemide. An alcoholic solution of furosemide forms a green compound under the action of p-dimethylaminobenzaldehyde, which changes to dark red. In the azo dye reaction, furosemide is hydrolysed with 1 mol/l HCl; then NaNO2 is added, then ammonium sulfamate and N-(1-naphthyl)ethylenediamine hydrochloride, and a red-violet azo dye forms. Ammonium sulfamate is added to destroy the excess sodium nitrite in the solution.

Reaction of furosemide with p-dimethylaminobenzaldehyde. An alcoholic solution of furosemide forms a green-coloured compound under the action of p-dimethylaminobenzaldehyde. This green compound then changes to a dark red colour. The observation is based on the change of colour from green to dark red.

t: Furosemide: steps of the azo dye reaction
n: Steps of the azo dye reaction. The first step is hydrolysis: furosemide is hydrolysed by heating with 1 mol/l HCl. In the second step, sodium nitrite is added to the solution. After a while, ammonium sulfamate is added, which destroys the excess nitrite. Then N-(1-naphthyl)ethylenediamine hydrochloride is added. As a result a red-violet azo dye forms.

Ultraviolet spectra of diuretics. Furosemide in alcohol gives a maximum at 274 nm, and its metabolite 4-chloro-5-sulfamoylanthranilic acid at 267 nm. Hydrochlorothiazide gives a maximum at 272 nm, acetazolamide at 264 nm, and ethacrynic acid at 278 nm. These values are given for solutions in alcohol.

t: UV spectra of diuretics: the figures
n: Ultraviolet spectra in figures. An alcoholic solution of furosemide gives a maximum at 274 nm, and the metabolite 4-chloro-5-sulfamoylanthranilic acid at 267 nm. Hydrochlorothiazide gives a maximum at 272 nm, acetazolamide at 264 nm, and ethacrynic acid at 278 nm. All for solutions in alcohol.

Hydrochlorothiazide and thin-layer chromatography developers. Hydrochlorothiazide gives a light blue precipitate with cobalt chloride, and a green-blue precipitate with copper (II) sulphate. Thin-layer chromatography systems: chloroform-benzene-2-propanol 2:4:1 and chloroform-ethyl acetate-2-propanol 10:5:1. According to the table, for hydrochlorothiazide mercury (II) sulphate and diphenylcarbazide are used, for furosemide iron (III) chloride, for acetazolamide Dragendorff reagent according to Munier, and for ethacrynic acid 0.5% potassium permanganate.

t: TLC developing reagents: matching to the substance
n: Matching developing reagents to the substance. For hydrochlorothiazide, a mercury (II) sulphate solution and diphenylcarbazide reagent are used. For furosemide, iron (III) chloride is used, and for acetazolamide Dragendorff reagent modified according to Munier. For ethacrynic acid, a 0.5% solution of potassium permanganate is used. Each substance is detected with its own developer.

Precipitation reactions of hydrochlorothiazide. Under the action of cobalt chloride solution, hydrochlorothiazide forms a light blue precipitate. Under the action of copper (II) sulphate, a green-blue precipitate forms. That is, the colour of the precipitate differs depending on the reagent: light blue with CoCl2, green-blue with CuSO4.

Standard solution of acetazolamide. 0.05 g of sample is placed in a 50 ml volumetric flask and dissolved in 5 ml of acetonitrile; the solution is made up to the mark. 1 ml of the prepared solution is taken and made up to the mark with acetonitrile in a 25 ml flask. The standard is prepared in the same order as the standard solution of furosemide.

t: Isolating acetazolamide from blood and urine
n: Isolating acetazolamide from blood and urine. Blood, 5 ml: brought to pH 3.0-4.0 with 0.1 N HCl, 2 g of 10% NaCl is added, and it is extracted twice with ethyl acetate-isopropanol 4:1. Urine: 25 ml of urine, 2 g of NaCl, 0.2 N HCl to pH=3.0-4.0; extracted twice with the same mixture. The extracts are passed through a filter with 5.0 g of dry Na2SO4 and dried at room temperature.

Let us compare the thin-layer chromatography of furosemide and acetazolamide. For furosemide, the system is chloroform-toluene-ethanol-25% ammonia 15:5:30:2, the developer is 5% iron (III) chloride, Rf=0.55. For acetazolamide, the system is benzene-2-propanol 8:2, the developer is Dragendorff reagent according to Munier, Rf=0.55. In both cases the test solution is applied beside the standard.

Isolating acetazolamide from liver. 50 g of minced liver and 50 ml of acetone are placed in a 100 ml flask and mixed for 1 hour on an electric shaker. A further 50 ml of acetone is added to the solid part and shaken for 30 minutes; the process is repeated twice. The acetone layers are centrifuged for 5 minutes at 3000 rpm. Saturated NaCl is added to the centrifugate and the acetone layer is evaporated; the aqueous part at pH 3.0-4.0 is extracted with ethyl acetate-isopropyl alcohol 4:1.

t: General scheme from object to TLC analysis
n: General scheme from the object to thin-layer chromatography analysis. An isolate is prepared from blood, urine or liver, the pH is adjusted and extraction is carried out. The extract is passed through a filter with dry Na2SO4 and dried. The dry residue is dissolved in acetone and applied to the start line of a Silufol plate. The eluate is taken from the spot and kept for further analysis.

The amounts for isolation from liver. 50 g of minced liver and 50 ml of acetone are mixed for 1 hour on an electric shaker. Re-extraction with 50 ml of acetone lasts 30 minutes. The centrifuge runs at 3000 rpm for 5 minutes. These figures are given for acetazolamide.

Chromatographic purification and analysis of acetazolamide. The residue is dissolved in 5 ml of acetone and 50 µg is applied to Silufol. The plate is run in the benzene-2-propanol 8:2 system to 10 cm. With Dragendorff reagent according to Munier, a brown spot forms, Rf=0.55. The eluate is dissolved in 10 ml of ethyl alcohol.

t: Purifying acetazolamide in a thin layer: steps
n: Steps of purifying acetazolamide in a thin layer. The dry residue is dissolved in 5 ml of acetone and applied to the start line of a Silufol plate as a band 1-2 cm wide, in an amount of 50 µg. The plate is run up to 10 cm in a chamber with benzene-2-propanol 8:2 and dried at room temperature. With Dragendorff reagent according to Munier, a brown spot forms, Rf=0.55. The eluate from the spot is transferred into 10 ml of ethyl alcohol.

Interpreting the result. The formation on the plate of a spot with Rf=0.55 at the same level as the standard indicates the presence of the corresponding drug in the test solution. For furosemide the developer is iron (III) chloride, for acetazolamide Dragendorff reagent according to Munier; fluorescence in ultraviolet light is also observed. The eluate obtained from the clean spot is kept for further ultraviolet spectrophotometric analysis.

Let us make an overall comparison of furosemide and acetazolamide. Furosemide is isolated with diethyl ether, acetazolamide with ethyl acetate-isopropyl alcohol 4:1. Furosemide is isolated from blood at pH=2.0, acetazolamide at pH=3.0-4.0. Furosemide is developed with FeCl3, acetazolamide with Dragendorff reagent. The furosemide eluate is dissolved in 25 ml, and the acetazolamide eluate in 10 ml of ethyl alcohol.

Review questions. First: the toxicological significance and classification of diuretic drugs. Second: the toxicological and narcological significance of furosemide and acetazolamide; write the formulae; which substance is the main metabolite of acetazolamide? Third: how is furosemide isolated from urine and blood? How is acetazolamide isolated from urine and blood? Fourth: explain the detection of furosemide and acetazolamide by thin-layer chromatography.

Conclusion. Furosemide: isolated with diethyl ether at pH=2.0 from blood and 2.0-3.0 from urine; in thin-layer chromatography in the 15:5:30:2 system with FeCl3, Rf=0.55; in the ultraviolet spectrum 274 nm. Acetazolamide: pH=3.0-4.0, ethyl acetate-isopropyl alcohol 4:1; system benzene-2-propanol 8:2, Dragendorff reagent according to Munier; in the ultraviolet spectrum 264 nm. Aqueous acetone method from liver: 50 g of liver, 50 ml of acetone, centrifuge 3000 rpm, 5 minutes.
